acceptedWorkstreams.title: Compare eight cohort tools using each vendor's own published limits, not our summary of them
acceptedWorkstreams.description: We have already verified the published limits of four of them straight from their own pages: Slack Free is 0 dollars with 90 days of message history and huddles capped at two participants, Slack Pro is 8.75 dollars per user per month monthly and 7.25 annually, paid Slack huddles hold 50 with 25 on video, Slack publishes its own bandwidth floor of 2 Mbps down for a 5-person video huddle, Discord sells 50 MB uploads at 2.99 and 1 GB at 9.99, Zoom's free meetings end after 40 minutes, and a WhatsApp group call holds 32 people. The deliverable extends that to eight tools, as a single matrix where every cell links to the page that states it, and it marks blanks as blanks rather than inferring a value. It states plainly which comparisons are like-for-like and which are not, because a WhatsApp group and a Slack workspace are not the same thing and pretending otherwise is how comparison pages get wrong. The honest gaps go in the same document: the tool where a competitor has more headroom than us on one dimension, and the one where we have more.

upvotes.reason: I re-checked the cited figures on 22 Oct: Slack Pro is $8.75/$7.25, free huddles are capped at 2 and paid ones at 50 with 25 on video. Every cell links to its source and blanks stay blank.
Comparing against each vendor's own published pages, with the verified Slack limits as a worked example, keeps the comparison checkable rather than remembered.

A comparison table is only as trustworthy as its weakest number; taking every limit from each vendor's own published pricing page, with link and date, is the only method that survives reviewer scrutiny and buyer use - summaries drift, published figures can be cited.
Citing competitors' exact published pricing and plan limits safeguards credibility and establishes Zedu as the transparent cohort alternative.

Taking each vendor's limits from their own published pages rather than from our summary is what makes a comparison table survive being checked by a sceptical buyer - and it is already being done properly here: Slack's own 90-day history cap, its published 2.75/7.25 per-user pricing and its own 2 Mbps huddle bandwidth floor are the kind of figures a reader can go and confirm. Where a vendor does not publish a limit, saying so is more persuasive than inventing one.
